title: When Giants Plant You, God Grows Harvests
summary:
# When Giants Plant You, God Grows Harvests

When the world buries you in darkness and silence, God sees not your ending but your beginning—a sacred planting that will bloom into a harvest far greater than your pain. Those moments when everyone has given up on you are precisely when an invisible champion is cheering not for who you were, but for the unstoppable person you're destined to become.
content:
You were not dying when they buried you. You were being planted.

There was a season when you believed you would never rise again. The voices around you had settled on your collapse. Friends had backed away. Family had stopped asking. Even your own voice — the one that once declared bold promises — had fallen silent. But somewhere beyond your line of sight, beyond the boundaries of your despair, there stood a champion. Not cheering for who you were. Cheering for who you would become. They saw your finish line when you could not even stand at the starting blocks. This is not sentimental encouragement. This is the pattern of God's prophetic design, and if the Church does not recover this fierce and holy function, we will continue to bury seeds we were meant to harvest.

The Prophetic Function of the Champion

Let us be clear from the outset: the champion is not a motivational speaker handing out participation trophies. The champion is a watchman stationed by God at the border of your future, refusing to let your present distort what Heaven has already declared over you. This is not a role born of human ambition. This is a sacred assignment, written into the very fabric of Scripture, embodied most powerfully in the relationship between Eli and Samuel, between Barnabas and Paul, between Moses and Joshua.

When Samuel was a child, the word of the Lord was rare in those days, and visions were infrequent (1 Samuel 3:1). The priesthood had grown corrupt. Eli's sons were wicked, and the lamp of God was about to go out in the temple. Yet Eli, aging and blind, recognized what he himself could no longer perform. He heard the boy running to him in the night and understood: God was calling someone else. Eli did not sabotage the next generation because his own had failed. He did not silence Samuel's voice because his own sons had disqualified themselves. Instead, he said, "Go and lie down, and if He calls you, say, 'Speak, Lord, for Your servant is listening'" (1 Samuel 3:9). This is the function of a champion. They do not compete with your calling. They coach you into it.

How many in the Body of Christ today are running to broken systems for confirmation, only to be told to go back to bed? How many prophetic voices are being silenced not by demons but by discouraged leaders who cannot see past their own disappointments? We need Elis who will train Samuels. We need Moseses who will commission Joshuas, even when their own feet will not cross the Jordan.

The Parable of the Unfinished Marathon

Let me give you a parable.

There was a runner who entered a race with great confidence. The route was long, twenty-six miles winding through hills and heat, but she had trained. She had prepared. She believed she had what it took to finish. But somewhere around mile eighteen, her body betrayed her. Her knees buckled. Her vision blurred. She collapsed on the side of the road, certain she was done.

The other runners passed her. Some glanced with pity. Others did not look at all. A few slowed down just long enough to say, "You gave it a good try." But one runner — a woman she had never met — stopped completely. This woman was not a medic. She was not race staff. She was another competitor. And stopping meant forfeiting her own time, her own placement, her own goal. But she knelt beside the fallen runner and said something strange: "I've seen you cross that finish line."

The collapsed runner looked at her in confusion. "You don't even know me."

"I know," the champion said. "But I've been where you are. And I've learned something about this race. The finish line is not just ahead of you. It's inside you. It was placed there before you ever started running. Now get up."

She did not pull her to her feet. She did not carry her. She simply stood, extended her hand, and waited. And when the fallen runner finally gripped that hand and rose, the champion began running beside her — not ahead, not behind, but with her. They crossed the finish line together. One had sacrificed her time. The other had discovered her tenacity. Both finished what they started, and both understood something the crowd did not: the race was never about speed. It was about refusal.

This is what champions do. They interrupt their own race to call you back into yours.

Barnabas and the Ministry of the Second Chance

The early Church had a man named Joseph, whom the apostles called Barnabas, which means "son of encouragement" (Acts 4:36). But Barnabas was not a cheerleader. He was a prophet with a peculiar gift: he could see finish lines that others could not. When Saul of Tarsus — the murderer of Christians, the destroyer of the faith — claimed to have encountered Jesus on the Damascus road, the Church recoiled in terror. They did not believe him. They did not trust him. They saw only his history, not his future.

But Barnabas saw differently. He took Saul and brought him to the apostles, vouching for his conversion, declaring the legitimacy of his encounter with Christ (Acts 9:27). Without Barnabas, we may never have known the Apostle Paul. Without Barnabas, thirteen epistles might have remained unwritten. Without Barnabas, the theology of grace that has shaped two thousand years of Christian thought might have died in the suspicion of a frightened church.

Do you understand what this means? It means your future may be locked behind someone else's willingness to champion you. It means the finish line God has prepared for you may require a Barnabas to unlock the door. And it also means this: you may be the Barnabas that someone else is desperately waiting for.

Later, when John Mark abandoned Paul and Barnabas during their first missionary journey, Paul wrote him off. He refused to take him on the second journey. Paul saw a quitter. But Barnabas saw a finisher in the making. So Barnabas took Mark and invested in him, trained him, restored him (Acts 15:37-39). And years later, Paul himself would write, "Get Mark and bring him with you, because he is helpful to me in my ministry" (2 Timothy 4:11). The one Paul rejected became the one Paul requested. Why? Because a champion refused to let a stumble define a destiny.

You Cannot See Your Own Finish Line

Here is a truth the enemy does not want you to grasp: you cannot see your own finish line from the middle of your mess. It is spiritually impossible. When you are in the valley, the mountain is invisible. When you are in the storm, the shore is obscured. This is why God places champions in your life — not to do the work for you, but to hold the vision for you when your own sight fails.

Moses could not see the Promised Land from the wilderness, but God gave him a vision of it from the mountain (Deuteronomy 34:1-4). David could not see the throne from the cave of Adullam, but Samuel had already anointed him king (1 Samuel 16:13). Peter could not see his restoration after his denial, but Jesus had already prayed for him and prepared breakfast on the beach (Luke 22:32, John 21:12). The common thread? Someone else held the vision while they endured the process.

This is not weakness. This is design. God built the Body of Christ to function as a relay, not a solo sport. We are meant to carry each other's vision when the weight becomes too much. We are meant to speak life into dead places. We are meant to prophesy to dry bones and watch them rise (Ezekiel 37:4-10).

If you are in a season where you cannot see your finish line, you are not disqualified. You are being prepared for a champion to find you. And if you have already crossed a finish line that nearly destroyed you, then turn around. Someone behind you is collapsing. And you have been given eyes to see what they cannot.

The Charge: Become a Champion or Find One

The Church today is filled with runners who have stopped mid-race, convinced they were never meant to finish. They sit on the side of the road, watching others pass, whispering to themselves, "I tried. I failed. It's over." Meanwhile, the enemy celebrates, because he knows something we have forgotten: a stopped runner is more dangerous to the kingdom than one who never started. Why? Because the stopped runner had momentum. They had movement. They were close. And if they ever rise again, they will run with a fury the comfortable will never understand.

So here is the prophetic charge, and I speak it with the urgency of one who has watched too many seeds rot in the ground because no one watered them: you must either become a champion or find one. There is no third option. If you are strong, stop running alone. Turn around and call someone forward. If you are weak, stop hiding in shame. Lift your head and look for the one who sees you differently than you see yourself.

God is not interested in a Church full of isolated finishers. He is building a company of champions who understand that their victory is incomplete until they've pulled someone else across the line. This is the gospel. This is love. This is the commandment Jesus gave us: "Love one another as I have loved you" (John 13:34). And how did He love us? He saw our finish line when we were still dead in our sins. He championed us to the cross. He refused to let our collapse define our destiny.

Now go and do the same.

Find the one who is falling and speak to their future. Call them by the name God gave them, not the one their failure whispered. Refuse to let them quit three steps from victory. And if you are the one falling, hear this: someone is coming. A champion is already walking toward you. They have been assigned by Heaven to see what you cannot. Do not close your eyes. Do not surrender to the voice of defeat. Your finish line is closer than you think.

The race is not over. The call has not been revoked. And the God who began a good work in you will be faithful to complete it (Philippians 1:6). Not because you are strong enough. But because He has stationed champions at the borders of your future, and they refuse to let Hell steal what Heaven has already purchased.

Get up. Your champion sees you. And your finish line is waiting.

title: God Sees You: The Power of Being Truly Known
summary: In a world that makes you feel invisible, God sees every tear, every struggle, and every act of faithfulness you thought went unnoticed—and He's calling you out of the darkness into the transformative power of being truly known. This is the radical truth that will shatter the loneliness you've carried: you were never invisible, and that recognition has the power to remake your entire life.
content:
You have spent too many years convinced that you are invisible.

You have walked into rooms believing no one truly notices. You have labored in silence, thinking your work, your struggles, your tears, and your faithfulness go unseen. You have whispered your prayers into the dark, wondering if even God remembers your name. But here is the truth that will undo every lie you have believed: You are seen. You are known. And you are being called forth.

The God who numbers the hairs on your head, who records your tears in His bottle, who carved your name into the palms of His hands—this God has never once looked away from you. Not for a moment. Not even when you looked away from yourself.

The Shepherd Who Sees One

There is something astonishing in the way Jesus tells the story of the lost sheep. Ninety-nine are safe in the fold, but the shepherd leaves them all to find the one that wandered. Not because the one is more valuable. Not because it earned special attention. But because that one mattered. (Luke 15:4-7)

Do you understand what this means? It means that when you feel like the smallest, least significant person in the Kingdom—when you are certain that everyone else is more gifted, more noticed, more called—Jesus leaves the crowd to search for you. He knows your name. He knows where you are. He knows what brought you to this place of hiding. And He comes, not with condemnation, but with the kind of pursuit that only love can sustain.

The religious leaders criticized Him for this. They could not comprehend a God who would abandon the many to rescue the one. But this is precisely the scandal of grace. You are not lost in a crowd to God. You are not a statistic, not a case number, not one voice drowned out by louder ones. You are the one He is searching for right now.

And when He finds you—oh, when He finds you—He does not scold you for wandering. He lifts you onto His shoulders, rejoicing. (Luke 15:5)

Known Before You Knew Yourself

David, the shepherd boy who became king, wrote these words from a place of overwhelming wonder: "O Lord, You have searched me and known me. You know when I sit down and when I rise up; You understand my thought from afar." (Psalm 139:1-2)

This is not casual knowledge. This is not the way you "know" a stranger's face in a crowd. This is intimate, exhaustive, perfect knowing. God knows your thoughts before you think them. He knows your words before you speak them. He knows the wounds you have never shared with anyone, the fears that wake you at three in the morning, the dreams you barely admit to yourself.

And still—still—He calls you His own.

Let me paint you a picture. Imagine a master potter standing before a lump of clay. The clay has been sitting in the corner of the workshop for months, overlooked, unformed, seemingly useless. But when the potter finally picks it up, he does not see what everyone else sees. He sees what it will become. He knows the vessel hidden inside. He has already imagined its shape, its purpose, its beauty.

This is how God sees you. Not as you appear in this moment—tired, uncertain, unfinished. He sees you as you are becoming. He sees the calling woven into your very being. Before you were born, before you took your first breath, He set you apart. Jeremiah heard these words: "Before I formed you in the womb I knew you, and before you were born I consecrated you; I appointed you a prophet to the nations." (Jeremiah 1:5)

Jeremiah protested. "I'm too young. I don't know how to speak." But God did not ask for qualifications. He asked for availability. Because the calling is not about what you bring to the table—it is about what God has already placed inside you.

Called Forth from Hiding

There was a man who lived among the tombs. The people of his town knew him only as the wild man, the demon-possessed one, the one who could not be bound even with chains. He was violent, tormented, naked, crying out day and night. Everyone avoided him. Everyone except Jesus.

When Jesus stepped off the boat, this man came running—not to attack, but because something deep within him recognized the One who could set him free. And Jesus did not recoil. He did not see a monster. He saw a man. A man created in the image of God, trapped under layers of darkness and pain. And Jesus called forth the true person buried beneath the chaos. (Mark 5:1-20)

After the deliverance, after the demons were cast out, the man sat at Jesus' feet, clothed and in his right mind. The townspeople were terrified—not of the demons, but of the transformation. They begged Jesus to leave. But the man? The man begged to follow Jesus. And here is what Jesus said: "Go home to your friends and tell them how much the Lord has done for you, and how He has had mercy on you." (Mark 5:19)

Jesus called him forth. Not just from the demons. From the tomb. From the identity the world had assigned him. From the shame and the isolation. Jesus called him into purpose.

Maybe you have been hiding in your own kind of tomb. Maybe people have labeled you: "broken," "too much," "not enough," "too old," "too young," "too damaged." Maybe you have accepted those labels as permanent truth.

But I tell you today—you are being called forth. Not someday. Not when you get yourself together. Now. Right now, in the middle of the mess, Jesus is speaking your name. He is not waiting for you to clean yourself up. He is calling you out so that He can do the cleaning.

The One Who Sees in Secret

There is a phrase Jesus uses that should stop us in our tracks. He says, "Your Father who sees in secret will reward you." (Matthew 6:4, 6, 18) He repeats it three times in one teaching—about giving, praying, and fasting. Why? Because so much of your faithfulness happens in secret.

You show up when no one is watching. You serve when no one applauds. You choose obedience in the small moments, the hidden moments, the moments that will never make it to a stage or a social media post. And you wonder sometimes if it even matters.

It matters.

God sees. Every act of love when you are exhausted. Every moment you choose patience when everything in you wants to snap. Every prayer you whisper over your children, your spouse, your friends. Every time you say no to the temptation that no one else would even know about. Every tear you cry in worship when you think no one is paying attention.

God sees in secret. And He does not forget.

Think of Hagar, the Egyptian servant who ran into the wilderness, pregnant and desperate. She was seen by no one who mattered—or so she thought. But God met her there. And she gave Him a name no one had used before: El Roi—the God who sees me. (Genesis 16:13)

You are not invisible. You never have been.

Parable of the Buried Seed

Let me tell you a story.

There was once a gardener who planted a seed in a dark corner of his garden, far from the pathways where visitors walked. The seed lay in the soil for weeks, unseen, unnoticed, doing its quiet work beneath the surface. No one knew it was there.

Other plants in the garden grew tall and beautiful, drawing admiration. People pointed and praised. The buried seed heard nothing. Saw nothing. It began to wonder if it had been forgotten.

But the gardener had not forgotten. Every morning, he watered that corner. Every evening, he checked the soil. He knew exactly where the seed was, exactly what it needed, exactly when it would break through.

And then one morning, a green shoot pierced the surface. Small. Fragile. But alive. The gardener smiled, because he had been watching all along. And in time, that plant—planted in the hidden place—bore fruit that fed many.

You are that seed. Your season of hiddenness is not abandonment. It is preparation. God has been watching. Watering. Waiting for the exact right moment to call you forth into the light.

The Call Is Now

Paul wrote to Timothy, a young leader who struggled with insecurity: "God has not given us a spirit of fear, but of power and of love and of a sound mind." (2 Timothy 1:7) This was not a suggestion. It was a declaration of identity. Timothy, you are not defined by your fear. You are defined by what God has placed in you.

The same is true for you.

You have been seen. From the very beginning, you have been known. And now, right now, you are being called forth. Not because you have arrived. Not because you are perfect. But because the Kingdom needs what God has placed inside you.

The world does not need another person pretending to have it all together. The world needs you—authentic, broken open, healed by grace, walking in the authority of one who has been found by the Shepherd.

So lift your head. Step out of the shadows. Let the labels fall. Let the lies die. You are not who they said you were. You are who God says you are.

You are seen.

You are known.

You are called forth.

Your Charge

Today, I am asking you to do something that may feel terrifying: believe that you matter. Not in some distant, theoretical way. But now. In this season. In this place. Believe that the God who calls stars by name (Isaiah 40:26) has also called you by name. Believe that the Good Shepherd is lifting you onto His shoulders even now, rejoicing that He has found you.

Stop waiting for permission. Stop waiting to feel ready. Stop waiting for someone else to notice you. God has already noticed. And He is calling you forth into the purpose He designed you for before the foundation of the world.

Speak it aloud if you need to: "I am seen. I am known. I am called forth."

Now walk in it. The world is waiting. The Kingdom is waiting. And the Shepherd who sought you is smiling, because He always knew you would rise.

title: When God Believes in You More Than You Do
summary: When doubt whispers that you're beyond redemption, God is still whispering your name—believing in the person you could become even when you've stopped believing in yourself. In your darkest moment of self-abandonment, there is One who refuses to write you off, not because you've proven yourself worthy, but because His love doesn't work on a merit system.
content:
You almost walked away, didn't you? Not from your job or your marriage or your city — from you. From the version of yourself God says you could become. You looked in the mirror and saw all the failures stacked up like unpaid bills, and you thought: Maybe everyone else was wrong about me. Maybe I'm not who they thought I was. But here's the truth that will shatter your resignation and rebuild your hope: Someone refused to give up on you. And it wasn't because you earned it. It was because He saw something in you that you couldn't see in yourself.

There is a relentless love in the heart of God that doesn't quit when you quit. It doesn't tire when you're tired. It doesn't look at your seventh failure and say, "Well, that's enough chances." While you were measuring your worth by your performance, Someone was measuring your worth by His blood. And He has been standing at the door of your discouragement, knocking — not once, not twice, but every single morning — because the One who refused to give up on you knows that your story isn't finished yet.

The Scandal of Unearned Persistence

Let me tell you about a farmer who had a field. In this field, he planted a vineyard — good soil, good seed, good sunlight. He did everything right. But one section of that vineyard refused to produce. Year after year, he'd walk past those barren vines, and his workers would say, "Cut them down. They're taking up space. They're draining resources from the good vines." But the farmer wouldn't do it. He'd prune them again. He'd fertilize the soil again. He'd water them again. His workers thought he was foolish. His neighbors thought he was wasteful. But the farmer kept saying, "Not yet. One more season. Let me try one more thing."

This isn't just a story. This is your biography.

Jesus told a version of this in Luke 13:6-9, a parable about a fig tree that hadn't produced fruit for three years. The owner said to cut it down. But the vinedresser — the one who worked the soil, who knew that tree intimately — said, "Sir, let it alone this year also, until I dig around it and fertilize it. And if it bears fruit, well. But if not, after that you can cut it down." The vinedresser refused to give up. Not because the tree deserved it. But because he believed in one more season.

That vinedresser is Jesus. And He's been digging around your roots when you thought you were too far gone.

You see, we live in a world that quits on people. Performance drops, potential fades, and the relationship gets severed. That's how the kingdom of this world operates. But the Kingdom of God operates on a different economy — one where grace isn't given because you earned it, but because He is generous. "Or do you despise the riches of His goodness, forbearance, and longsuffering, not knowing that the goodness of God leads you to repentance?" (Romans 2:4). His refusal to quit on you isn't a reward for your righteousness. It's an invitation into it.

When You Couldn't Even Believe in Yourself

There's a moment in every believer's life when you realize you've become your own enemy. Not the devil. Not the world. You. You're the one whispering, "You'll never change. You'll always be this way. You're too old, too broken, too far behind." And in that moment, the most dangerous thing isn't your sin — it's your unbelief in God's persistence.

Peter knew this. After he denied Jesus three times, after he cursed and swore that he never knew Him, Peter didn't just feel guilty — he felt finished. He went back to fishing (John 21:3). Not because he loved fishing, but because he thought his calling was over. He thought Jesus would wash His hands of him. But Jesus didn't. Jesus cooked him breakfast. Jesus asked him three times, "Do you love Me?" — once for every denial, once for every wound, once for every lie Peter believed about himself. And then Jesus said, "Feed My sheep" (John 21:17). In other words: You're not done. I'm not done with you. Get back to work.

Jesus refused to give up on Peter, even when Peter had given up on Peter.

Maybe you're reading this and you feel like Peter felt — like you've disqualified yourself. Like you said the wrong thing, did the wrong thing, walked away from the right thing one too many times. Let me tell you what Jesus is saying to you right now, in this moment: "I didn't die for the version of you that never messes up. I died for the version of you that does — and then gets back up because I won't let you stay down."

The Apostle Paul said it this way: "He who has begun a good work in you will complete it until the day of Jesus Christ" (Philippians 1:6). Not might complete it. Not could complete it. Will complete it. Because the One who started the work is the One who finishes it. And He doesn't start things He doesn't intend to finish.

The Difference Between Quitting and Resting

Now, let me be clear about something: there's a difference between giving up and letting go. There's a difference between quitting in defeat and resting in trust. Some of you are exhausted because you've been trying to finish what only God can complete. You've been gripping your own transformation with white knuckles, thinking that if you don't hold yourself together, you'll fall apart. But faith isn't about holding yourself together. It's about letting the One who holds all things together do what only He can do.

Jesus said, "Come to Me, all you who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest" (Matthew 11:28). He didn't say, "Come to Me and I'll give you a to-do list." He said He'd give you rest. But rest doesn't mean inactivity — it means trust. It means you stop carrying what He's already carrying. It means you stop trying to save yourself and let the Savior do the saving.

I've observed countless people who walk away from their faith not because they stopped believing in God, but because they stopped believing God still believed in them. They got tired of failing. Tired of falling short. Tired of praying the same prayers and struggling with the same sins. And somewhere in that weariness, they made a decision: "If I can't be who I'm supposed to be, I'll just stop trying."

But here's what the enemy doesn't want you to know: your weariness is not evidence of your failure. It's evidence of your humanity. And your humanity is exactly what Jesus came to redeem. He didn't come for people who had it all together. He came for people who were falling apart — and He said, "I'll hold you together."

The One Who Sees What You Will Become

There's a stunning moment in the Gospels that we often read too quickly. Jesus meets Simon for the first time, and immediately — without a resume, without a background check, without a trial period — He renames him. "You are Simon the son of Jonah. You shall be called Cephas (which is translated, A Stone)" (John 1:42). In other words: "Right now, you're Simon. But I see Peter. Right now, you're unstable. But I see a rock."

Jesus didn't call him what he was. He called him what he would become.

And He's doing the same thing with you.

When you see your inconsistency, He sees your potential. When you see your track record, He sees your destiny. When you see your limitations, He sees the limitless power of His Spirit working in you. He's not looking at who you are right now and deciding whether you're worth the investment. He's looking at who you will be when His grace finishes its work — and He's already decided you're worth everything.

That's why He refused to give up on you. Not because you convinced Him. But because He knows the end from the beginning, and He's seen the finished version of you — the one that looks like Him.

What Happens When You Let Him Stay

So what do you do with this relentless love? What do you do when you realize that Someone has been fighting for you even when you stopped fighting for yourself?

You let Him stay.

You stop running. You stop hiding. You stop performing and pretending and protecting the image you think you need to maintain. You come out of the shadows and you say, "Jesus, if You're still here, if You still want me, then I'm Yours. All of me. The good parts and the broken parts. The progress and the setbacks. The victories and the defeats. I'm not giving up anymore — because You never gave up on me."

And here's what happens when you do that: you don't just survive. You flourish. Because the same power that raised Jesus from the dead starts working in you (Ephesians 1:19-20). The same Spirit that hovered over the chaos in Genesis and brought order out of nothing starts hovering over your chaos — and He starts creating again. New habits. New thoughts. New desires. New strength.

The Apostle Paul, who once murdered Christians and called himself the chief of sinners, wrote these words toward the end of his life: "I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith" (2 Timothy 4:7). How did a man who started as a persecutor finish as a preacher? Because Someone refused to give up on him. Jesus knocked him off his horse, blinded him with light, and said, "I have plans for you" (Acts 9). And Paul spent the rest of his life responding to that relentless love.

That same love is after you.

The Charge: Don't You Dare Quit Now

So let me say this as clearly as I can: don't you dare quit now. Not after everything God has already brought you through. Not after every prayer He's already answered, every door He's already opened, every battle He's already won on your behalf. The enemy wants you to believe that you've reached your limit — that you've used up all your chances, that God's patience has run out. But that's a lie straight from the pit of hell.

The truth is this: the One who began a good work in you is still working. The One who called you is still calling. The One who loved you enough to die for you loves you enough to finish what He started. He's not done with you. He's not tired of you. He's not looking for a reason to disqualify you.

He's looking for a reason to promote you.

So stand up. Shake off the discouragement. Reject the lie that you're too far gone. Jesus didn't refuse to give up on you so that you could give up on yourself. He refused to give up on you so that you could walk in the fullness of everything He died to give you — freedom, purpose, identity, power, and love that doesn't quit.

You are not who you were. You are becoming who He says you are. And the same Jesus who refused to give up on Peter, on Paul, on every broken person who ever called on His name — that same Jesus is refusing to give up on you.

So don't quit. Don't walk away. Don't close the door on your destiny because you had a bad season. Let the Vinedresser do His work. Let the One who sees the finished version of you complete what He started. Because your story isn't over. It's just getting to the good part.

And the One who refused to give up on you is about to show you why.

title: When Exhausted Faith Meets Another's Strength
summary:
# When Exhausted Faith Meets Another's Strength

In moments when our own faith runs dry and our knees buckle beneath the weight of life, God often sends us another believer whose strength becomes the very hands that hold us up—transforming the moment we would have fallen into the moment we discover we were never meant to stand alone. This is the raw, physical reality of Christian community: not inspiration or encouragement from a distance, but the literal, life-saving presence of another's unwavering faith catching us when ours gives out.
content:
I have observed something that shakes me to the core every time I encounter it: the exact moment when a believer's strength gives out completely—and the hands of another believer rise up beneath their arms.

It is not a metaphor. It is not poetic exaggeration. It is the literal difference between standing and collapsing. Between continuing and quitting. Between faith held and faith abandoned. And here is what I have come to understand through years of studying the Scriptures and watching the people of God walk through fire: God never designed you to carry certain battles alone. The idea that spiritual maturity means solitary strength is a lie from the pit, and it has crippled more believers than perhaps any other deception in the modern church.

Let me take you back to a moment recorded in the book of Exodus—a battle scene that most people read and miss entirely.

The Battle That Required Three People

Moses stood on a hill. Below him, Joshua led the armies of Israel against the Amalekites. And as long as Moses held up his hands, Israel prevailed. But when his hands grew heavy and dropped, Amalek prevailed (Exodus 17:11). This is where most sermons focus on Moses—his intercession, his endurance, his role as mediator. But I want you to see what happened next, because this is where the real revelation sits.

"But Moses' hands grew weary, so they took a stone and put it under him, and he sat on it, while Aaron and Hur held up his hands, one on one side, and the other on the other side. So his hands were steady until the going down of the sun. And Joshua overwhelmed Amalek and his people with the sword" (Exodus 17:12-13).

Did you catch it? Moses could not finish the battle alone. His arms gave out. The text does not say he was weak in faith. It does not say he doubted God. It says his hands grew weary. This is not a character flaw—this is humanity. And God did not rebuke Moses for his weariness. Instead, He provided Aaron and Hur.

Here is the thesis that will confront everything you have been taught about self-sufficiency in the faith: There are seasons when your obedience to God will require someone else's strength under your arms, and there is no shame in that—only surrender to the way God designed His Body to function.

The Lie of the Lone Ranger Christian

I have observed in modern Christianity a toxic obsession with individualism dressed up as faith. We celebrate the lone intercessor, the solitary saint, the one who "stands alone when no one else will." We sing songs about walking through the valley by ourselves. We preach sermons that make it sound like dependence on another believer is a sign of immaturity.

But that is not what Scripture teaches.

Paul wrote to the Galatians:

"Bear one another's burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ" (Galatians 6:2).
This is not a suggestion. This is not Plan B for weak Christians. This is the law of Christ—the governing principle of how His Body operates. If you refuse to let someone hold your arms when you cannot hold them yourself, you are robbing them of the privilege of fulfilling Christ's law in their own life. You are not being strong—you are being proud.

Let me be blunt: when you insist on going it alone, you are not demonstrating great faith. You are denying the design of the Kingdom. God built the Church as a Body precisely because no single member contains everything needed for victory. The eye cannot say to the hand, "I have no need of you" (1 Corinthians 12:21). And neither can you.

I have seen too many believers collapse under weights they were never meant to carry alone. I have seen marriages end, ministries implode, and faith shipwrecked—not because the person lacked devotion, but because they refused to let anyone else step into the gap.

When Your Arms Drop: A Modern Parable

Let me tell you about something I have observed—a story that will help you see this truth with fresh eyes.

There was a man who worked in construction, and he was known for his strength. He could carry loads that other men needed two or three people to move. He took pride in this. It was part of his identity. One day, he was tasked with holding a steel beam in place while the crew secured it with bolts. The beam weighed hundreds of pounds. He gripped it, lifted it, positioned it. But the crew was delayed. The bolts were the wrong size. He had to hold the beam longer than expected.

Minutes passed. His arms began to shake. Sweat poured down his face. His supervisor saw this and called for two other men to come help. But the man refused. "I've got it," he said through gritted teeth. "I don't need help." His pride would not allow him to admit his arms were failing. And then it happened—his strength gave out completely. The beam dropped. It crushed his foot. He was out of work for months. The job was delayed. The whole crew suffered because one man refused help that was freely offered.

Now hear this: How many spiritual beams have dropped in your life because you refused to let someone hold your arms? How many battles have been lost not because God's power was insufficient, but because you rejected the delivery system He provided—another believer standing beside you?

The Theology of Held Arms

Let's go deeper into what Scripture actually reveals about this principle, because I want you to see that this is not just practical wisdom—this is covenant theology.

When Aaron and Hur held up Moses' arms, they were not taking over his role. They were not replacing him. They were enabling him to fulfill his calling. Moses was still the intercessor. His hands were still raised. But their strength became his strength. This is the mystery of the Body of Christ.

Paul explained it this way:

"Now you are the body of Christ and individually members of it" (1 Corinthians 12:27).
A body does not function with one part doing everything. The legs walk, but they need the eyes to see where they are going. The hands work, but they need the brain to direct them. When one part is weak, the other parts compensate. This is not weakness—this is design.

Jesus Himself modeled this. In the Garden of Gethsemane, He took Peter, James, and John with Him and said,

"My soul is very sorrowful, even to death. Remain here and watch with me" (Matthew 26:38).
The Son of God—fully divine, fully human—asked His disciples to stay near Him in His darkest hour. He did not need them to pray for Him. He needed them to be there. He needed their presence. Their proximity. Their witness.

If Jesus did not walk through His hardest moment alone, why do you think you should?

The Practical Reality: Who Holds Your Arms?

Here is where this becomes uncomfortably personal. I want you to stop reading for a moment and ask yourself a real question: Who in your life has permission to hold your arms when they drop?

Not who would you call in an emergency. Not who you might text if things got really bad. I am asking: who has seen you weak? Who knows where you are struggling right now? Who has you told, "I cannot do this anymore—I need you to help me stand"?

If you cannot name at least two people, you are in danger. Not because you are a bad Christian, but because you are living outside the structure God designed for your protection.

I have observed that the enemy does his best work when he can isolate a believer. He does not need to destroy your faith if he can just convince you to carry your burdens alone. Isolation is the incubator for every destructive thought pattern, every hidden sin, every creeping doubt. But when you are held by the arms of a brother or sister who refuses to let you fall, the enemy's strategy collapses.

Ecclesiastes puts it plainly:

"Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their toil. For if they fall, one will lift up his fellow. But woe to him who is alone when he falls and has not another to lift him up!" (Ecclesiastes 4:9-10).

Woe. That is a strong word. It is not a gentle warning—it is a pronouncement of danger. Being alone when you fall is not just unfortunate. It is perilous to your soul.

The Shame We Must Destroy

Now let me address the thing that stops most people from allowing their arms to be held: shame.

There is a voice that whispers, "If you were really strong in faith, you would not need this. If you were really walking with God, you would be able to handle this on your own. Asking for help is admitting defeat."

That voice is a liar.

Needing help is not defeat. It is humility. And humility is the soil in which every Kingdom seed grows. James wrote,

"God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble" (James 4:6).
When you admit you cannot hold your arms up any longer, you are positioning yourself to receive God's grace—and that grace often comes through the hands of another believer.

Pride says, "I must be strong enough." Humility says, "God is strong enough, and He sends His strength through His people." Which voice are you listening to?

The Call to Be an Arm-Holder

But this teaching cuts both ways. If you are reading this and your arms are not the ones that are dropping—if you are in a season of strength right now—then hear this word clearly: You are called to watch for the arms that are falling around you.

Aaron and Hur did not wait for Moses to ask. They saw. They acted. They positioned themselves on either side and held. This is what it means to be the Body. You do not wait for someone to articulate their need perfectly. You do not wait for them to say the magic words. You see the trembling. You see the strain. And you move.

I have observed too many believers who are willing to hold arms only if asked directly. But most people who are drowning do not have the strength to shout for help. They are using every last ounce of energy just to keep their head above water. You must develop eyes to see the silent struggle. You must become the kind of person who shows up before the collapse.

This requires presence. It requires attention. It requires the willingness to inconvenience yourself for the sake of another's survival. But this is not optional for those who claim to follow Jesus. He said,

"By this all people will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another" (John 13:35).
And love does not wait to be summoned. Love watches. Love anticipates. Love holds.

The Charge: Stand and Be Held

So here is what I am saying to you today, with the authority of the Word and the urgency of one who has seen too many fall unnecessarily:

If your arms are dropping, stop pretending they are not. Call someone today. Text them. Show up at their door. Say the words out loud: "I need you to hold my arms. I cannot do this alone anymore." It is not weakness—it is wisdom. It is not defeat—it is trust in the way God designed His Kingdom to function.

And if you are strong right now, look around. Who is struggling in silence? Whose arms are shaking? Do not wait for them to ask. Move toward them. Position yourself beside them. Hold them steady until the battle is won.

title: God's Love Sees Past Our Brokenness
summary:
# God's Love Sees Past Our Brokenness

In our darkest moments of struggle and shame, God's love doesn't wait for us to become worthy—it meets us exactly where we are, broken and drowning, with a compassion that transforms our very ability to survive. This radical, unconditional acceptance becomes the lifeline we didn't know we needed, teaching us that true redemption begins not when we fix ourselves, but when we finally believe we are loved anyway.
content:
You were drowning in your own life when someone reached into the water — not to pull you into their boat, but to remind you that you could still breathe. They saw what was killing you, and they loved you anyway. They didn't love you because you promised to change. They didn't love you after you cleaned yourself up. They loved you while you were still a mess. And somehow, that impossible love became the very thing that finally gave you permission to live.

Here is the thesis of this hour: The love that looks past our mess is not permissive — it is prophetic. It does not excuse sin; it exposes the person God has always seen beneath it. This is the scandalous nature of agape love, the foundational truth of the gospel, and the operational heartbeat of authentic discipleship. When we understand this love — when we have truly received it and learned to give it — we become living epistles of the grace that once saved us. We become believers who believe in other believers, even when they cannot yet believe in themselves.

The Doctrine of Divine Disregard

Let us reason together from Scripture. In Romans 5:8, Paul declares a reality so staggering it should never become routine in our hearing: "But God demonstrates his own love for us in this: While we were still sinners, Christ died for us." Do you see the scandal embedded in that sentence? The cross was not a reward for repentance. It was not the final transaction after we completed our part of the bargain. Christ did not die for the cleaned-up version of humanity. He died while we were still sinners — still lying, still stealing, still hating, still proud, still lost in the very darkness that was killing us.

This is what I call the Doctrine of Divine Disregard. God looked past the mess. He saw the mess — make no mistake — but He looked past it to see what He had originally created and what He intended to restore. He did not pretend the sin wasn't there. He simply refused to let the sin define the final verdict on who we were. The mess was real. The love was greater. The cross proves that the value God placed on humanity was not determined by our current condition, but by His eternal intention.

When someone loves you while you are still in your mess, they are operating in the same spirit that moved God toward Calvary. They are not enabling your destruction. They are refusing to define you by it. There is a holy distinction here that the religious mind often misses: to love someone past their mess is not to say the mess doesn't matter — it is to say the person matters more.

The Parable of the Cracked Vessel

Let me tell you a story. There was once a potter who made a vessel of great beauty. It was formed with care, designed for a specific purpose, shaped by skilled hands. But while still drying in the sun, a careless traveler knocked it from its place, and the vessel fell. It cracked — not shattered, but broken enough that it could no longer hold water the way it was meant to.

Other potters passed by. Some shook their heads. "What a waste," they said. "It will never be what it was supposed to be." Some offered advice. "You should have been more careful. You should have been placed somewhere safer." Some offered religious comfort: "Perhaps this is the vessel God intended all along — a broken one. Embrace your brokenness."

But the original potter returned. He picked up the cracked vessel and looked at it — not with pity, not with disappointment, but with recognition. "I know what this was supposed to be," he said. "I know what it still is, even if no one else can see it." He took the vessel back to his workshop. He did not pretend it was unbroken. He did not ignore the cracks. But he also did not discard it. He remade it — sometimes adding gold to the cracks, sometimes reshaping it entirely, but always with the original design in his mind. And when he was finished, the vessel held water again. It bore the marks of what it had been through, yes. But it fulfilled its purpose.

This is what happens when someone believes in you past your mess. They are not pretending you are not broken. They are reminding you that broken is not your final identity. They see what the Potter sees. And often, that kind of love is the very catalyst the Potter uses to begin the rebuilding.

The Apostolic Pattern: Confrontation Rooted in Conviction

Now we must address a tension. Some will say, "Does this mean we tolerate sin? Does this mean we never confront, never correct, never hold others accountable?" Absolutely not. But here is where the Church has often erred: we have learned to confront without conviction — conviction, that is, of the person's belovedness.

Look at how Paul addressed the Corinthian church. This was a church full of mess. Sexual immorality. Division. Arrogance. Lawsuit-happy believers dragging each other before pagan courts. Drunkenness at the Lord's Supper. Chaos in worship. If there was ever a congregation that deserved to be written off, it was Corinth. And yet, how does Paul open his letter? "To the church of God in Corinth, to those sanctified in Christ Jesus and called to be his holy people." (1 Corinthians 1:2)

Do you see what he did? He identified them not by their mess, but by their calling. He called them sanctified and holy — not because they were acting sanctified and holy, but because that is what God had declared them to be in Christ. Paul did not ignore their sin. He confronted it head-on throughout the letter. But he confronted it from a foundation of belovedness, not from a posture of condemnation. He believed they could become what God said they were, even while they were still acting like what they had been.

This is the apostolic pattern. Love that looks past the mess does not avoid the mess. It simply refuses to let the mess have the final word. It speaks to identity before it addresses behavior. It reminds before it rebukes. It believes before it corrects.

Someone Saw You When You Couldn't See Yourself

If you are reading this, there is a high probability that you are alive in the faith today because someone loved you past your mess. Maybe it was a parent who kept praying when you kept running. Maybe it was a friend who sat with you in the rubble of your bad decisions and said, "I'm still here." Maybe it was a pastor who didn't kick you out when you confessed what you'd done. Maybe it was a stranger who looked you in the eye when everyone else looked away.

They didn't fix you. They didn't solve your problems. But they saw you. And in seeing you, they reflected the gaze of the Father — the One who has always looked at you with eyes unclouded by your failures, the One who named you beloved before you ever did a single thing to earn it.

In Luke 15, we find three parables about lostness: the lost sheep, the lost coin, and the lost son. The religious leaders grumbled because Jesus welcomed sinners and ate with them (Luke 15:2). In response, Jesus told stories about searching, about finding, about celebration. But notice the central message of all three parables: the lost thing had value even while it was lost. The sheep was worth searching for while it was still wandering. The coin was worth lighting a lamp and sweeping the house while it was still under the couch. The son was worth running toward while he still smelled like pig slop.

This is the love that looks past the mess. It does not wait for you to find your way home before it starts running. It does not wait for you to clean yourself up before it embraces you. It sees the mess. It runs anyway.

Becoming the Kind of Love You Once Needed

Now we arrive at the turn. If you have been loved past your mess, you have been entrusted with a sacred assignment: become that love for someone else. This is not optional. This is not for the mature believers only. This is the essence of discipleship itself. In John 13:34, Jesus said, "A new command I give you: Love one another. As I have loved you, so you must love one another."

As I have loved you. Not as you feel like it. Not as they deserve it. Not when they get their act together. As I have loved you — which is to say, sacrificially, unconditionally, prophetically. The love you received is the love you are now commanded to give.

There is someone in your life right now who is drowning. You know who they are. They are the ones everyone else has written off. They are the ones who keep failing, keep relapsing, keep making the same destructive choices. They are the ones whose mess is so obvious that even they have stopped believing they can change. And you — yes, you — have been positioned by the Holy Spirit to be the love that looks past their mess.

This does not mean you enable. This does not mean you pretend the mess isn't there. This does not mean you allow yourself to be abused or manipulated. Boundaries and love are not enemies; they are partners. But it does mean you refuse to give up on them. It means you keep praying when everyone else stops. It means you keep speaking their true name — beloved, redeemed, called, chosen — even when they are living like none of those things are true.

The Call: Love Like You Were Loved

So here is the charge, believer. Stop waiting for people to clean themselves up before you love them. Stop requiring proof of change before you extend grace. Stop letting their mess determine whether they are worth your time, your prayers, your presence. You were a mess once. You were loved anyway. That love changed you — not because it excused your sin, but because it reminded you who you really were underneath it.

Now go and do likewise. Find the ones everyone else has given up on. Sit with them. Speak life over them. Believe for them when they cannot believe for themselves. You are not responsible for fixing them — that is the Holy Spirit's job. But you are responsible for reflecting the Father's gaze, for being the incarnational presence of the love that once saved you.

Paul wrote to the Ephesians: "Be imitators of God, therefore, as dearly loved children and walk in the way of love, just as Christ loved us and gave himself up for us as a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God." (Ephesians 5:1-2) Do you hear it? Walk in the way of love. Not the way of judgment. Not the way of conditional acceptance. Not the way of "I'll love you when you deserve it." Walk in the way of love — the same love that looked past your mess and saw a child of God.

This is the gospel. This is the heartbeat of the Kingdom. This is how the world will know we are His disciples — not by our doctrine alone, not by our worship services alone, but by our love. The reckless, illogical, inconvenient, cross-shaped love that sees people not as they are, but as they were created to be. The love that believed in you when no one else did. The love that now lives in you, waiting to be poured out on the next broken vessel the Potter is preparing to restore.

Go. Be that love. Someone is waiting for you to see past their mess and remind them who they really are.
